chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding His words
He said: 'It means the grasping of the imagination. Do you not see His words:
'There has come to you Insight from your Lord' [6:104]

It does not mean the sight of the eyes. 'Whoever therefore sees, it is for his own soul' — it does not mean seeing with his physical eye. 'And whoever is blind, it shall be against himself' — it does not mean the blindness of the eyes. Rather, He meant the grasping of the imagination,

just as it is said: so and so has insight in poetry, and so and so has insight in jurisprudence, and so and so has insight in Dirhams, and so and so has insight in clothes. God is more magnificent than that He should be seen with the eye.'

key_terms.إحاطة الوهم: Grasping of the imagination/intellect — the cognitive faculty that attempts to encompass God
key_terms.الأبصار: Visions/sights — plural of basar, here interpreted as the comprehending capacity of imagination, not physical eyesight
key_terms.بصائر: Insights/clear proofs — intellectual perspicacity, contrasted with physical sight

ai.seo_question: Can God be seen with physical eyes according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) explains that the Quranic phrase 'visions cannot comprehend Him' (6:103) does not refer to physical sight but to the grasping capacity of the human imagination and intellect. He substantiates this with the immediately following verse (6:104), where 'insight' (basar) clearly refers to intellectual understanding, not physical vision — just as Arabic usage speaks of someone having 'insight' in poetry, law, or commerce. This is a fundamental Shia theological argument against the belief that God can be seen with physical eyes (ru'yat Allah), affirming divine transcendence.
word_analysis: it is for his own soul

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Isa, from Ibn Abu Najran, from Abdullah Bin Sinan,
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullahasws regarding Hisazwj Words [6:103] Visions cannot comprehend Him.
He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The grasping of the imaginations. Do you not see His<sup>azwj</sup> Words
[6:104] There has come to you Insight from your Lord?

It does not Mean the insight of the eyes whoever will therefore see, it is for his own soul, it does not Mean the visualising with his eyes and whoever will be blind, it shall be against himself, it does not mean the blindness of the eyes. But rather, it Means the grasp of the imagination,

just as it is said, ‘So and so has insight in the poetry, and so and so has insight in the understanding, and so and so has insight in the Dirhams, and so and so has insight in the clothes’. Allah<sup>azwj</sup> is more Magnificent than that He<sup>azwj</sup> should be seen with the eye’.
en.sarwar: 9. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Isa from ibn abu Najran from ‘Abdallah ibn Sinan from Imam abu ‘Abdallah (a.s.) who has said the following about the words of Allah.
“No mortal eyes can see Him, but He can see all eyes. He is All-kind and All-aware.” [6:103]
It means within what is called al-Wahm which in terms of the degrees of knowledge is less than fifty percent. Consider the words of Allah in:
“Clear proofs have certainly come to you from your Lord.. .” [6:104]

It does not mean eye-witnessed knowledge. Also consider, “Whosoever sees clearly, it is to his own gain.” (ibid) does not mean seeing with the eyes and in “Whosoever is blind, it is to his own loss’ (ibid ). Blindness does not mean deprivation of eye-sight. It means within the range of Wahm (mentioned above).

As is commonly said, so and so is very keen-sighted in matters of poetry, and so and so is very keen-sighted in religion and jurisprudence. So and so has a keen eye for money, and so and so an eye for clothes. Allah is far great and above being eye-witnessed by people.”
